result.question:
Agentic AI workloads at the edge — definition, taxonomy, and resource characterization — for an edge-SoC vendor like NXP i.MX (serving consumer, industrial, and automotive markets; product range from a small NPU + Cortex-A55 part up to a high-end part with 16× Cortex-A720, a ~500 eTOPS NPU, and 256-bit LPDDR5X). The vendor's VP wants to benchmark "what agentic on the edge means and its performance requirements," prompted by Qualcomm's latest Snapdragon "agentic phone" announcements (e.g. "use the phone to buy me concert tickets"). Answer the following with cited sources:

(1) DEFINITION — What does "agentic" concretely mean on-device at the edge versus in the cloud? Rigorously distinguish (a) an agent that ORCHESTRATES A FIXED SET OF PRE-TESTED on-device skills/tools [intent-parse → plan → execute known skills → synthesize, no new code generated] from (b) an autonomous agent that GENERATES AND RUNS NOVEL CODE to accomplish open-ended tasks. Which model do shipping agentic edge/phone products actually use today (Snapdragon X Elite / 8-series agentic features, Apple Intelligence, Google Gemini Nano on-device, Samsung)? Is code-generation ever executed on-device as a shipped product, or is it always the fixed-skill-orchestration model?

(2) USE CASES — Concrete, real or seriously-proposed edge-agentic use cases for: robotics, smart-camera edge boxes, industrial field-service/maintenance, and automotive (in-cabin assistant + ADAS-adjacent). For each, which are "today's tech" (a single perception model with a command front-end) versus genuinely agentic (multi-step orchestration of several skills)?

(3) TAXONOMY + BENCHMARK SELECTION — How should agentic tasks be categorized, and what would a representative 5-task benchmark set for edge agentic look like? What distinguishes a task that genuinely needs an LLM "agent" from one that is just a perception pipeline with a natural-language command front-end?

(4) RESOURCE CHARACTERIZATION METHODOLOGY — How do you measure an agentic workload's demand decomposed into CPU vs memory-bandwidth (LPDDR5X) vs NPU/accelerator? Specifically how do the phases of multi-step LLM-driven orchestration map to hardware: LLM prefill (compute/TOPS-bound, parallel) vs LLM decode (memory-bandwidth-bound, serial, KV-cache grows with context) vs tool-call sub-workloads (ASR/Whisper, OCR, vision CNN, vector-DB/RAG retrieval)? Which metrics matter (end-to-end latency, time-to-first-token, tokens/sec, tool-call count, peak vs sustained bandwidth, energy per task)?

(5) EXISTING BENCHMARKS — Survey existing agentic benchmarks (AgentBench, tau-bench, WebArena, AndroidWorld / mobile-agent benchmarks, MLPerf edge/mobile/client). Do ANY measure on-device RESOURCE COST (not just task success rate)? What is the gap, and what would a credible "edge agentic resource benchmark" need that existing ones lack?

(6) THE KEY ARCHITECTURAL QUESTION — Is there a measurable difference between the edge processor "being the agent" (a single agent that fully understands a bounded mission — a front-end captures a natural-language prompt and engineers it into a task the edge agent already knows how to execute) versus running MULTIPLE cooperating agents on the edge? When is multi-agent justified on constrained edge silicon versus a single well-scoped agent, given the resource cost (extra LLM context, memory, bandwidth) of each additional agent?
result.summary: Every shipping on-device agentic product today uses the FIXED-SKILL-ORCHESTRATION model (intent-parse → plan → invoke a pre-defined, structurally-validated set of tools/skills → synthesize), NOT autonomous on-device novel-code generation. Google's Gemini Nano exposes four fixed GenAI capabilities via per-task LoRA adapters; Apple's ~3B 2-bit on-device model is explicitly not a general chatbot and uses constrained tool-calling that guarantees no hallucinated tool names/args; both tier complex work to the cloud. The resource signature of multi-step LLM orchestration is dominated by the DECODE phase, which is memory-bandwidth-bound (not TOPS/compute-bound): prefill is compute-bound and parallel, but decode is autoregressive/serial with a KV-cache that grows linearly with context, and in real agentic traces decode consumes 91-98.6% of LLM time because high cross-turn context reuse means little re-prefill — meaning for an edge SoC the binding constraint is LPDDR5X bandwidth, not the 500-eTOPS NPU. Existing agentic benchmarks (AgentBench/tau-bench/WebArena/AndroidWorld class) measure task SUCCESS RATE in effectively unconstrained environments and do not measure on-device resource cost; a small cluster of 2025-2026 papers (AgentSLABench, AgBench, AgentPerfBench, RooflineBench) is only now beginning to add memory/bandwidth/compute/energy profiling and local-vs-hybrid-vs-cloud tradeoffs, confirming the benchmark gap the VP is asking about. On concurrency/multi-agent: adding agents is expensive — prefix-cache hit rate collapses from ~98% to 16-26% and throughput drops up to 66% under concurrent agent load — so a single well-scoped agent is favored on constrained silicon unless the mission genuinely requires parallel independent context.

findings.claim: DEFINITION (Q1): Every shipping on-device agentic edge/phone product uses the fixed-skill-orchestration model — a bounded set of pre-tested, structurally-validated skills/tools invoked via plan→execute→synthesize — NOT an autonomous agent that generates and runs novel code on-device. Google Gemini Nano exposes exactly four fixed GenAI capabilities (summarization, proofreading, rewriting, image description) via ML Kit, each backed by a feature-specific LoRA adapter. Apple's ~3B on-device model is quantized to 2 bits-per-weight via QAT and is explicitly NOT a general-purpose chatbot — it is specialized for a fixed task set and uses constrained tool-calling that guarantees structural correctness and prevents hallucinated tool names/arguments. No shipping product executes open-ended on-device code generation.
findings.evidence: Four unanimous (3-0) primary-source claims converge. Google's Android Developers Blog (Aug 2025) enumerates the four fixed GenAI features and states each uses 'LoRA adapters trained specifically for each GenAI API feature' = discrete pre-trained skills (even the more-flexible GenAI Prompt API is NL prompting, not code-gen). Apple's own tech report (arXiv 2507.13575, July 2025) states the on-device model 'is not designed to be a chatbot for general world knowledge,' is specialized for summarization/entity-extraction/text-understanding/refinement/short-dialog/creative-content, and that its Foundation Models framework 'can guarantee the structural correctness of tool calls by preventing hallucinated tool names or arguments' and 'handles the potentially complex call graphs of parallel and serial tool calls.' Converges on: shipped edge agentic = bounded fixed-skill orchestration, not autonomous code generation.

findings.claim: DEFINITION/ARCHITECTURE (Q1,Q6): Shipping edge assistants explicitly TIER work between a small on-device model for low-latency/low-resource tasks and a larger cloud model for complex tasks. Apple splits a ~3B on-device model against a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts (PT-MoE) server model on Private Cloud Compute. Benchmark evidence confirms no single deployment architecture (local/hybrid/cloud) dominates: local-only completes many tasks but underperforms cloud in success rate and speed, with the gap widening under concurrent load, while local wins on privacy and zero API cost.
findings.evidence: Apple tech report (arXiv 2507.13575, 3-0) confirms the on-device-vs-cloud PT-MoE tiering verbatim. AgBench (arXiv 2609.38652, two 3-0 claims) — an academic personal-AI-device benchmark over 162M data points by edge-computing researcher Blesson Varghese et al., mirrored on SSRN — states verbatim 'no single architecture performs best across task success, goodput, cloud cost, and data exposure' and that 'local-only execution generally has lower task success and longer completion times than cloud-only, especially as concurrency increases.' Concurrency-widening gap independently corroborated (Oracle 1,000-agent benchmark; device-cloud latency studies).

findings.claim: RESOURCE METHODOLOGY (Q4): LLM inference decomposes into a compute/TOPS-bound prefill phase (input tokens processed in parallel, high weight reuse) and a memory-bandwidth-bound decode phase (autoregressive, serial, each step depends on prior tokens, KV-cache grows linearly with context). At 16-bit the operational intensity of decode is ~1 FLOP/Byte; because edge accelerators have peak-compute-to-bandwidth ratios far exceeding 1 (a ~500-eTOPS NPU on ~100 GB/s LPDDR5X gives a roofline ridge in the thousands of FLOP/byte), compute cores sit idle waiting for weight/KV-cache loads, yielding low model FLOPs utilization. Growing KV-cache traffic pushes decode deeper into the memory-bound region, making MQA/GQA attention optimizations necessary. The correct methodology decomposes each decoder layer into constituent ops, computes per-component FLOPs and DRAM bytes → operational intensity (FLOPs/byte) → roofline throughput ceiling, enabling phase-to-hardware mapping.
findings.evidence: Six unanimous (3-0) primary-source claims converge from two independent papers. RooflineBench (arXiv 2602.11506, Bi et al. Feb 2026) gives prefill-compute/decode-memory split verbatim, OI_decode≈1 FLOP/Byte at 16-bit, P_peak/BW≫1 → idle cores → low MFU, and KV-cache pushing decode 'deep into the severe memory-bound region' requiring MQA. AgentPerfBench (arXiv 2609.34683, Sept 2026) independently quantifies an 8-28x prefill-vs-decode operational-intensity gap, shows chat workloads memory-bound (OI_eff=181) vs coding-agent compute-bound (OI=2,409) on an H100 (ridge=295), and documents the layer-decomposition methodology verbatim (OI_j=FLOPs_j/DRAMBytes_j; P_roof=min(P_peak, OI×BW)). The mobile/edge survey (arXiv 2510.00078) corroborates KV-cache growing linearly with sequence length as a primary edge bottleneck. Textbook-consensus physics, multiply corroborated, non-marketing.

findings.claim: RESOURCE METHODOLOGY (Q4): In real agentic LLM workloads the decode phase dominates 91.0-98.6% of LLM compute time (prefill only 1.4-9.0%) because high cross-turn context reuse (empirical prefix-cache-hit 84.6-99.5%) means most input tokens are cached rather than re-prefilled — so agentic execution is memory-bandwidth-bound, not prefill/compute-bound. Agentic workloads are NOT merely long-prompt workloads: they are long-tailed across two INDEPENDENT dimensions — turn count and accumulated context length — so resource demand cannot be characterized by prompt size alone. Tool-call sub-workloads are heterogeneous and must be profiled as distinct categories (file inspection, shell/code execution, web retrieval, delegated subagent work — and by extension on edge: ASR/Whisper, OCR, vision CNN, vector-DB/RAG retrieval), each with different latency and failure profiles.
findings.evidence: Three claims from the primary workload-characterization paper (arXiv 2605.26297v2, 'Agentic AI Workload Characterization'). The 91.0-98.6% decode-dominance figure and 84.6-99.5% cache-hit are verbatim; 'agentic workloads are not simply long-prompt workloads' and the two-independent-dimensions (turn count vs context growth; SWE-bench Pro 69K-80K-token contexts) are verbatim with independence explicitly stated. Tool-heterogeneity verbatim ('tool use is not a single systems category'). Two of three claims 3-0; the decode-dominance claim 2-1 (the dissent noted non-LLM tool calls add compute-bound time to whole-task runtime, but the claim correctly scopes to 'LLM compute time'). Caveat: the enumerated tool categories are from coding/software agents, not edge perception pipelines — but tool-call heterogeneity holds as a general principle.

findings.claim: MULTI-AGENT ARCHITECTURAL QUESTION (Q6): Running multiple concurrent agents on constrained silicon is measurably expensive. Under increasing agent concurrency, GPU/accelerator memory pressure causes prefix-cache hit rate to collapse from ~98% to 16-26% and reduces generation throughput by up to 66%, because the accumulated KV-cache exceeds memory and forces prefix recompute. This quantifies the resource cost of each additional agent's context and favors a single well-scoped agent on edge silicon unless the mission genuinely requires parallel independent contexts.
findings.evidence: Claim 3-0 from arXiv 2605.26297v2 Table II: prefix-cache hit 98.85%→16.78% (Terminal-Bench) and 98.53%→25.17% (DABStep) under rising concurrent agent jobs; gen throughput 30.08→16.96→10.30 tok/s/req = 66% drop. Corroborated by TraceLab (arXiv 2606.30560) and XPerf (arXiv 2608.20370). IMPORTANT CAVEAT: measured on 2x H100 NVL 80GB with vLLM — the mechanism (KV-cache memory pressure → cache thrashing → throughput collapse) transfers to edge, but the specific numbers do NOT transfer to LPDDR5X edge silicon and would need re-measurement on target hardware. The direction is the answer to Q6: multi-agent multiplies the memory/bandwidth cost that is already the edge bottleneck.

findings.claim: EXISTING BENCHMARKS GAP (Q5): Existing agentic benchmarks focus on single-turn chatbot interactions or task success rate in effectively unconstrained environments and do NOT measure on-device resource cost. The mobile/edge survey evaluates agentic tasks only with planning correctness, termination error rate, and task success rate, listing energy merely as a MAC/FLOPs proxy with no resource-aware benchmark cited. A new cluster of 2025-2026 papers is only now filling the gap: AgentSLABench adds Docker-enforced CPU/memory/time/network budgets and a six-dimension per-episode profile (correctness, latency, cost, compute, network, safety); AgBench measures local/hybrid/cloud deployment on success/latency/API-cost/data-exposure; AgentPerfBench adds saturation-based, real-trace-derived measurement. A credible edge-agentic resource benchmark needs what these still lack: measured on-device energy-per-task, peak vs sustained LPDDR5X bandwidth, and the CPU/NPU/bandwidth decomposition of each orchestration phase on real edge silicon.
findings.evidence: Four claims. AgentPerfBench (arXiv 2609.34683, 3-0): existing inference benchmarks 'primarily focus on simple single-turn chatbot-style interactions,' set sequence lengths as fixed user variables not real traces, and 'none sweeps the full load curve to locate saturation.' Mobile/edge survey (arXiv 2510.00078, 3-0): evaluation = planning correctness/termination error/task success; energy only as MACs/FLOPs; no resource-aware agentic benchmark cited. AgBench (arXiv 2609.38652, 3-0): 'existing benchmarks are inadequate for systematically characterizing these trade-offs across devices.' AgentSLABench (arXiv 2608.00805, medium/2-1): six-dimension Docker-enforced profile; its characterization of the closest prior work (APBench measures only latency+token usage, lacks memory/network/compute) is self-sourced and unverified. NOTE: a broader claim that 'NO existing benchmark measures resource cost' was REFUTED 0-3 — the accurate statement is that mainstream success-rate benchmarks don't, while this new 2025-2026 cluster is beginning to.

findings.claim: TAXONOMY / EDGE-AGENTIC FRAMING (Q2,Q3,Q6): The edge-agentic problem is fundamentally a resource-characterization problem — the field frames agentic AI on mobile/edge as bounded by memory, energy, bandwidth, and latency, i.e. a fundamental tension between growing foundation-model complexity and limited deployment resources. The canonical agentic workflow decomposes into Perception, Cognition, Memory, Agent-Learning, Action, and System-scheduling stages and uses chain-of-thought goal decomposition plus ReAct think-act-observe loops — which is definitionally the fixed-skill orchestration/planning model (plan → act via known tools → observe), not on-device novel-code generation. This provides the taxonomy spine: a task genuinely needs an LLM 'agent' when it requires multi-step goal decomposition and orchestration across several skills; it is merely a perception pipeline with an NL command front-end when a single perception model answers directly.
findings.evidence: Two 3-0 claims from arXiv 2510.00078 ('Adaptive and Resource-efficient Agentic AI Systems for Mobile and Embedded Devices: A Survey,' Liu et al., Sept 2025). Verbatim: 'mobile and edge deployments remain constrained by memory, energy, bandwidth, and latency ... fundamental tension between the growing complexity of FMs and the limited resources of deployment environments.' Six-stage decomposition verbatim; CoT goal-decomposition ('High-level instructions ... decomposed into sub-goals via chain-of-thought reasoning') and ReAct ('interleaves think-act-observe trajectories') verbatim. The ReAct/CoT/tool-orchestration framing is the fixed-skill planning model, reinforcing the Q1 finding. Primary, current, on-topic survey.

result.caveats: (1) Concurrency/multi-agent numbers (prefix-cache 98%→16-26%, 66% throughput drop) were measured on datacenter GPUs (2x H100 NVL 80GB, vLLM), NOT on edge LPDDR5X silicon — the MECHANISM transfers but the specific numbers do not; direct re-measurement on i.MX-class hardware is required. (2) Roofline ridge-point figures (OI=181/2409, H100 ridge=295) are H100-specific; the ~500-eTOPS NPU on ~100 GB/s LPDDR5X gives a far higher ridge (~5000 FLOP/byte), which only STRENGTHENS the memory-bound conclusion for edge decode but should be computed with real i.MX NPU TOPS and real LPDDR5X bandwidth. (3) Several supporting papers (AgentSLABench, AgBench, AgentPerfBench, RooflineBench) are non-peer-reviewed 2026 arXiv preprints; AgentSLABench's characterization of competitor APBench is self-sourced and could not be independently verified (held to medium confidence). (4) The decode-dominance 91-98.6% figure scopes to LLM compute time only; on edge the non-LLM tool calls (ASR/OCR/vision CNN/RAG) add compute-bound and I/O-bound time to WHOLE-task latency and must be measured separately. (5) The tool-call taxonomy in the workload paper is drawn from coding/software agents (Bash/Edit/Read/WebFetch), not edge perception pipelines — the heterogeneity principle holds but the specific categories need re-mapping to ASR/OCR/vision/RAG for the edge case. (6) Time-sensitivity: Snapdragon 8-series/X-Elite and Samsung agentic specifics were NOT directly confirmed by a surviving primary claim — the shipping-product evidence that survived verification is Google (Gemini Nano) and Apple; the Qualcomm/Samsung 'agentic phone' claims that prompted the VP remain to be verified against primary Qualcomm/Samsung sources.
openQuestions: What is the actual on-device architecture of Qualcomm Snapdragon 8-series/X-Elite 'agentic' features and Samsung's agentic phone (the specific prompt for this research)? No surviving primary claim confirmed them as fixed-skill vs code-gen — only Google and Apple were verified. The 'buy me concert tickets' demo almost certainly uses cloud+fixed on-device skills, but this needs direct Qualcomm/Samsung primary-source confirmation.

What are the measured CPU/NPU/LPDDR5X-bandwidth/energy-per-task numbers for a representative multi-step agentic workload on actual i.MX-class silicon (small NPU+A55 part vs the 16x A720 / 500-eTOPS / 256-bit LPDDR5X high-end part)? All quantitative resource data that survived is from H100/datacenter or generic roofline — the edge measurement does not yet exist and IS the benchmark gap NXP would need to fill.

What does a concrete, validated 5-task edge-agentic benchmark set look like (Q3), with per-task phase decomposition into prefill/decode/tool-call sub-workloads? The methodology (layer-level FLOPs/DRAM-bytes → OI → roofline) is established, but no source provided a ready-made edge-specific 5-task suite spanning robotics / smart-camera / field-service / in-cabin automotive.

At what mission complexity does multi-agent become justified on constrained edge silicon versus a single well-scoped agent? The resource COST of extra agents is quantified (cache collapse, throughput drop), but the crossover point — the task characteristics where parallel agents' benefit outweighs the memory/bandwidth penalty on edge — was not established by any source.

refuted.claim: No existing agentic benchmark measures resource cost — standard agent benchmarks (WebShop, ALFWorld, SWE-bench, GAIA, AgentBench, ToolBench) report only task accuracy in unconstrained environments with effectively unlimited compute, memory, and API budgets, and none measure both success and resource consumption under production-realistic constraints.
